To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
online social media can lead to labor market discrimination, and that employers search only superficially in the online profiles they consult.

1) Social network profiles are used as an additional signal in the screening process.2) This screening occurs early in the process.3) The signal is used superficially, and the screening stops as soon as the recruiter finds a reason to discard the applicant.4) This superficial screening is costly to employers, and the cost is high enough to explain the gap between the test applicant and the control.

(i) recruiters do not use Facebook to discriminate against applicants, but (ii) they discriminate against applicants based on the signal we manipulated in Facebook, and (iii) they do so early in the hiring decision process, before they have access to the application material, but (iv) they do so superficially, as a change in the layout of Facebook reduces the effect of our signal.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the use of social media as a tool to discriminate in the labor market.
the question of whether online social networks can be used as a screening device by recruiters.
the question of the extent of labor market discrimination based on online social networks.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
online profiles are indeed used for screening, that this occurs early on, but that the screening is superficial and does not go beyond the information available in the front page.
the use of social media for hiring purposes is widespread and that it is likely to lead to discrimination, but that the extent of this practice depends on the depth of search by recruiters.
the use of Facebook as an additional screening tool for employers has a significant negative impact on the job prospects of applicants, and that the depth of this search is very limited.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
social networks are indeed used by recruiters, but only to the extent that they are easily accessible.
recruiters are using online profiles as a screening tool but are only using the most salient information, which is also the most likely to be discriminatory.
online social networks are used as a screening device in the hiring process, but the search is not thorough enough to capture all the available information.
The main takeaway from our work is that
social media can indeed be a source of labor market discrimination.
social media can indeed be used to screen applicants and lead to discrimination.
online social networks can be used by employers to discriminate applicants.
